title: The king's regret
hookLine: Ajatasattu confesses; the Buddha says had he not killed his father he would have seen the truth that night

cards: The teaching is over. The Buddha has walked the king all the way from the honored slave to the end of the taints. The lamps are still burning in the pavilion.

And King Ajatasattu, who rode out because he wanted peace in his heart, does two things. First he says the familiar words that close these discourses: excellent, as if something overturned had been set upright.
He goes for refuge. And then he says what he came carrying.

teach.b: Lord, he says, a transgression overcame me. Foolish, confused and unskillful as I was, for the sake of the throne, I took the life of my father, a good man, a righteous king.
May the Blessed One accept my confession, so that I may restrain myself in the future. The Pali word is accaya: a transgression, a going beyond the line. The Buddha's answer is direct.
Yes, great king, a transgression overcame you. He doesn't soften the deed. But since you see it as a transgression, and make amends in line with the dhamma, we accept it.

teach.h: SEEN AS WRONG, WE ACCEPT IT
teach.b: For this is growth in the noble discipline: to see a wrong as wrong, make amends, and restrain yourself in the future. The king rises, bows, and leaves.
And then the Buddha says something to the monks that is hard to hear.

teach.h: THIS IS GROWTH IN THE DISCIPLINE
HE WOULD HAVE SEEN, BUT FOR THAT
teach.b: If he had not taken his father's life, the clear eye of the dhamma would have opened in him tonight, on that very seat. The discourse holds two things at once.
Confession is real, and welcomed; it's called growth, not humiliation. And the deed is real too; it has left a mark that one honest night can't remove.

The king came for peace of heart and received something more sober: the path is still open to him, but he will walk it carrying what he did. Later tradition remembers Ajatasattu as a supporter of the community.
The canon doesn't pretend the night erased the past. It just doesn't close the door.

how: Buddhist monastics confess offenses to one another in regular ceremonies, and lay Buddhists in some traditions acknowledge wrongdoing and renew their precepts, following the pattern in DN 2: seeing a wrong as wrong, making amends, and resolving restraint.

o: a king's pardon given to a criminal
a ritual for washing away all guilt
a wrong, a going beyond the line

games.q: the king's regret: tap the pairs.
p: he is wounded, the Buddha says

s: the Buddha tells the king his deed doesn't matter now
he names it a transgression, accepts the confession, and later says it kept the king from seeing the truth that night.
confessing a wrong is called growth in the noble discipline
seeing it, making amends, and restraining oneself in future.
the king goes for refuge before he confesses
he says excellent, goes for refuge, and then confesses.

games.q: you're the Buddha. a king who killed his own father confesses it and asks you to accept his confession. what do you say?
o: it was a wrong, and since you see it so and make amends, we accept it.
games.why: the Buddha neither excuses nor rejects. he names the wrong, accepts the confession as growth, and only afterward tells the monks what the deed cost the king.

practice: Choose a small regret, something you can hold without being flooded, and name it plainly to yourself, with no excuses and no punishment: I did this.
Then rest with the three steps from the text, seeing it as a mistake, making amends if there's a way, intending to do differently, and let it simply be seen while you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Accaya. A transgression, a going beyond the line: the king's wrong, seen as wrong, confessed and accepted as growth, while the deed still leaves its mark.

orig.note: Pali accaya: a transgression, literally a going beyond. the word in the king's confession.

carryVoice: Your line: regret, confessed. Seeing a wrong as wrong is where growth begins. Rest well.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 2, Samaññaphala Sutta, the closing section
